title: Mary and Martha part 2
scripture_text: ’’As Jesus and his disciples were on their way, he came to a village where a woman named Martha opened her home to him. She had a sister called Mary, who sat at the Lord’s feet listening to what he said. But Martha was distracted by all the preparations that had to be made. She came to him and asked, “Lord, don’t you care that my sister has left me to do the work by myself? Tell her to help me!” “Martha, Martha,”the Lord answered, “you are worried and upset about many things, but few things are needed—or indeed only one. Mary has chosen what is better, and it will not be taken away from her.”
devotional:
Martha: -

‘She came to him…’ a more literal meaning of the phrase ephistemai in v. 40 can simply mean "to stand near or by," and even "to oppose.” It conveys the ideas of urgency, as of a soldier ready to go into battle on a moment’s notice or a guard who stands continually on alert for threat of enemy infiltration or attack. It is as if Martha feels a need to stand up for herself, so she bursts into the room totally exasperated with Jesus and Mary, she is frustrated and angry, and says, ‘Lord don’t you care?’ She begins to think wrongly about Jesus. ‘Lord don’t you care?’ At this time she is viewing Jesus as someone who is unconcerned about her and what she is feeling. When we stop believing that Jesus cares, we start to lash out at others. When Martha says, “Lord, don’t you care?” she really means to say, “Lord, you don’t care at all because if you did, you would have told Mary to go to the kitchen and help me.”

Martha is feeling neglected and abandoned by Jesus however, although she was feeling this way, her feelings were not communicating the truth.

She accused Mary of being the problem because she refused to recognise the problem in herself. ‘Lord don’t you care that my sister has left me?’ Martha does not see any problem with herself, but she blames those who are innocent of wrongdoing. The word for left, kataleipo, is a very strong word it means to be forsaken. The word was used to describe the leaving a loved one at death, it carries the idea of feeling bereaved. Martha was having a massive emotional over reaction to Mary, she was feeling like a victim, at this point she was out of control. Her emotions were clouding her judgment.

She tried to use Jesus as a means of fulfilling her agenda. ‘Tell her to help me.’ Luke uses a very unusual word to describe the help Martha asked for. The meaning of the word can best be illustrated when we think of carrying a huge log, have you ever tried to carry one by yourself? One end falls down, then the other end falls down and the whole thing swings this way and that. To carry a log is much easier if there are two people, one on each end. Martha was asking for a partner. The only other time the word is used is in Romans 8:26 speaking about the Help we receive from the Holy Spirit. What Martha really needed was for God to become her partner in work, however her failure to recognise this, meant that she placed impossible demands on other people and only increased the frustration and tension in the household. Martha’s mistake was not that she was working in the kitchen. Her mistake was rushing out and demanding Mary show her love in the same way.

Charles Hummell, wrote in Freedom from the Tyranny of the Urgent:

‘Tension and frustration mount when we are performing the wrong tasks or trying to cram too many of the right activities into a given period. A critical spirit develops and we begin to judge and condemn others for what they do or don’t do. Anytime you feel a wave of criticism gaining momentum in your spirit remember it’s completely out of line as far as God is concerned.’ [Charles Hummel. Priorities: Tyranny of the Urgent. Christian Basic Bible Studies. (InterVarsity Press, 1994)].

Martha’s biggest problem was that she lacked self-control. We may not be totally responsible for how the circumstances around us make us feel, but we are totally responsible for how we manage and control our responses and emotions. The Greek word for self-control egkrateia literally means a holding oneself in or the ability to take a grip of oneself. Plato uses egkrateia to refer to self-mastery. It is the spirit which has mastered its desires and its love of pleasure. Secular Greek uses egkrateia of the virtue of an Emperor who never lets his private interests influence the government of his people. Self-control is part of the fruit of the Spirit.

Self-control means mastering one’s emotions rather than being controlled by them.
prayer: Father sometimes we lose perspective because we have lost control of our emotions.
